latin.meaning: summit, peak, gable; highest point, pinnacle of honor or power
latin.forms: nom. fastīgium, gen. fastīgiī, dat. fastīgiō, acc. fastīgium, abl. fastīgiō (2nd decl. neuter)
latin.etymology: From *fastīgō (to make pointed), related to fastīgātus (sloping, pointed). Possibly connected to the root *bhasg- (to bind, make firm).
latin.literary_context: Cicero uses fastīgium frequently in his philosophical works and speeches to denote the apex of dignity or achievement. In De Oratore, he speaks of reaching the fastīgium of eloquence as the orator's ultimate goal.
latin.usage_example: Ad summum fastīgium glōriae pervēnit. — He arrived at the highest pinnacle of glory.
latin.did_you_know: In Roman architecture, fastīgium specifically referred to the triangular gable or pediment of a temple, making it both a literal and metaphorical peak. The word became synonymous with imperial dignity, as in fastīgium imperātōrium.

greek.forms: ἀναγκαῖος, -α, -ον (masc., fem., neut.); comparative ἀναγκαιότερος; superlative ἀναγκαιότατος
greek.etymology: From ἀνάγκη (necessity, constraint) + adjectival suffix -αῖος. The root ἀνάγκη itself derives from ἀνα- (intensive) + the verbal root of ἄγχω (to squeeze, strangle).
greek.literary_context: Aristotle uses τὸ ἀναγκαῖον extensively in the Nicomachean Ethics and Physics to distinguish what is necessary by nature from what is contingent. Plato employs the term in Republic Book 2 when Socrates discusses the necessary (ἀναγκαῖαι) versus unnecessary desires in building the ideal city.
greek.usage_example: Τὰ ἀναγκαῖα πρῶτον δεῖ παρασκευάζειν. — One must first provide the necessary things.
greek.did_you_know: Aristotle distinguished between simple necessity (ἁπλῶς ἀναγκαῖον) and hypothetical necessity (ἐξ ὑποθέσεως ἀναγκαῖον), a distinction that became foundational in medieval scholastic philosophy through Latin translations as necessarium simpliciter and necessarium ex suppositione.

french.forms: singular: la houle; plural: les houles
french.etymology: From Middle Dutch holle 'hollow, cavity' or related Germanic roots referring to hollow waves. Entered French maritime vocabulary in the 16th century.
french.literary_context: Baudelaire uses houle in 'L'Homme et la mer' from Les Fleurs du mal, where the sea's swell mirrors the turbulence of the human heart: 'Homme libre, toujours tu chériras la mer! / La mer est ton miroir; tu contemples ton âme / Dans le déroulement infini de sa lame, / Et ton esprit n'est pas un gouffre moins amer.'
french.usage_example: La houle berce le navire dans un mouvement régulier et profond. — The swell rocks the ship in a regular and deep motion.
french.did_you_know: In French maritime tradition, houle designates the long rolling waves that persist after a storm has passed, distinguishing it from vague (surface wave) or lame (breaking wave). Hugo exploited this distinction in Les Travailleurs de la mer to convey the ocean's lingering menace.

german.forms: die Verklärung, gen. der Verklärung, pl. die Verklärungen
german.etymology: From the verb verklären (to transfigure, to glorify), composed of the prefix ver- (indicating transformation) + klären (to clarify, from klar 'clear'). The word originally carried religious meaning (transfiguration of Christ) before expanding to aesthetic and philosophical contexts.
german.literary_context: Thomas Mann uses Verklärung throughout Der Tod in Venedig to describe Aschenbach's aesthetic transfiguration of Tadzio, transforming physical beauty into Platonic ideal. Nietzsche employs the term in Die Geburt der Tragödie when discussing how Apollonian art transfigures the terror of existence into beautiful form.
german.usage_example: Die Musik Wagners strebt nach der Verklärung des Leidens. — Wagner's music strives toward the transfiguration of suffering.
german.did_you_know: Schopenhauer identified Verklärung as the ultimate achievement of art, whereby aesthetic contemplation temporarily lifts us above the will's torment and grants us a vision of pure Ideas divorced from individual suffering.

oldenglish.meaning: word-hoard, treasury of words, vocabulary, mental storehouse of language
oldenglish.forms: nom./acc. sg. wordhord; gen. sg. wordhordes; dat. sg. wordhorde; nom./acc. pl. wordhord
oldenglish.etymology: Compound of word 'word' + hord 'hoard, treasure, store'. Proto-Germanic *wurda- + *huzdam. The metaphor of language as treasure was common in Germanic poetic diction.
oldenglish.literary_context: In Beowulf (line 259), the coastal guard speaks wisely from his wordhord: 'Æghwæþres sceal scearp scyldwiga gescad witan, worda ond worca, se þe wel þenceð' — a sharp shield-warrior who thinks well must know the distinction between words and deeds. The Exeter Book riddles also employ this term for mental eloquence.
oldenglish.usage_example: Onlēac his wordhord wide. — He unlocked his word-hoard widely.
oldenglish.did_you_know: The concept of wordhord reflects the Anglo-Saxon view that eloquence and wisdom were treasures to be accumulated and carefully dispensed, paralleling how literal gold-hoards were distributed by lords to worthy retainers in the mead-hall.

italian.meaning: to transmute, to transform, to change from one form or nature into another
italian.forms: Present: trasmuto, trasmuti, trasmuta, trasmutiamo, trasmutate, trasmutano. Past participle: trasmutato. Gerund: trasmutando.
italian.etymology: From Latin trans- (across, beyond) + mutare (to change). The prefix intensifies the sense of transformation, suggesting a complete change of nature or substance.
italian.literary_context: Dante uses trasmutare in Paradiso II.37-38 to describe the transformation of matter, explaining how Beatrice's face changed: 'Beatrice in suso, e io in lei guardava; e forse in tanto in quanto un quadrel posa e vola e da la noce si dischiava, giunto mi vidi ove mirabil cosa mi torse il viso a sé.' The verb appears again in Paradiso I.67-70 regarding Glaucus, who was transmuted into a sea god.
italian.usage_example: Trasumanar significar per verba non si poria; però l'essemplo basti a cui esperïenza grazia serba. - To trans-humanize cannot be signified in words; therefore let the example suffice for him to whom grace reserves the experience.
italian.did_you_know: Dante coined the verb 'trasumanar' (to transcend humanity) from 'trasmutare' in Paradiso I.70, creating one of Italian literature's most famous neologisms to describe the ineffable experience of spiritual transformation beyond human nature.

middleenglish.meaning: courteous, refined in manners, possessing the qualities of courtly behavior
middleenglish.forms: Positive: corteys; Comparative: more corteys; Superlative: moost corteys. Adverb: corteysly. Noun form: corteysie (courtesy).
middleenglish.etymology: From Old French corteis/curteis (courtly, elegant), derived from cort (court) + -eis (-ous). The Old French cort comes from Latin cohors, cohortis (enclosure, retinue). The term entered English after the Norman Conquest, carrying associations with aristocratic refinement and chivalric ideals.
middleenglish.literary_context: Chaucer uses corteys repeatedly in the Canterbury Tales to describe the Prioress (General Prologue, line 132): 'And she was cleped madame Eglentyne. Ful weel she soong the service dyvyne... And she was cleped madame Eglentyne. Ful corteys she was.' The Pearl-poet employs it in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight to describe the refined behavior expected of knights at Arthur's court.
middleenglish.usage_example: The knyght was corteys and of gentil port, and spak ful faire to alle maner folk. - The knight was courteous and of noble bearing, and spoke very graciously to all manner of people.
middleenglish.did_you_know: In medieval romance literature, corteys embodied an entire social code encompassing not just politeness but also generosity, loyalty, and refined speech. Chaucer sometimes uses the word ironically, as when describing characters whose corteys behavior masks less noble intentions.
